report:
## Does dexamethasone ensure survival for critically ill COVID-19 patients?

**Short answer: No — the evidence shows it reduces mortality risk on average, but it does not "ensure" survival, and its benefit is neither universal nor guaranteed.**

The RECOVERY trial, a large UK randomized controlled trial, found that dexamethasone reduced 28-day mortality by about one-third in patients requiring mechanical ventilation, and by about one-fifth in patients requiring supplementary oxygen (https://www.recoverytrial.net/news/low-cost-dexamethasone-reduces-death-by-up-to-one-third-in-hospitalised-patients-with-severe-respiratory-complications-of-covid-19). Crucially, the trial also reported that dexamethasone showed **no mortality benefit** — and possibly harm — in patients not requiring oxygen support (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436).

A WHO-led prospective meta-analysis pooling seven randomized trials (including RECOVERY) confirmed corticosteroids were associated with lower 28-day all-cause mortality among *critically ill* COVID-19 patients as a group, compared with usual care (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2770279). However, this is a statistical association across populations — a reduction in relative risk of death, not a guarantee of individual survival. Even in the treated groups, substantial proportions of critically ill patients still died; the trial itself estimated that treating around 8 ventilated patients prevents one death, meaning most patients did not personally benefit in a life-or-death sense (https://www.recoverytrial.net/news/low-cost-dexamethasone-reduces-death-by-up-to-one-third-in-hospitalised-patients-with-severe-respiratory-complications-of-covid-19).

**Conclusion:** Dexamethasone is an effective, evidence-based treatment that lowers mortality risk for critically ill, oxygen-dependent COVID-19 patients, but it does not ensure survival for any individual patient, is ineffective (or possibly harmful) in less severe disease, and outcomes still depend on other factors like timing, disease severity, and comorbidities.
